_meta.title: AI Challenge of the Week
_meta.rotationNote: Rotation by ISO calendar week; after week 12 it restarts at week 1. The next twelve challenges are prepared by week 10.

challenges.role: HR lead at an 80-person engineering company
challenges.scenario: The CFO wants a salary benchmark against five competitors in three days. You have public sources, two hours for a first analysis and no data analyst.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Brief with role, region and five columns: competitor, role and level, salary range, source, confidence. 2. Collect a few documented public records per competitor within site terms; never present estimates as payroll facts. 3. Let the model extract ranges and flag uncertain values. 4. Check the three most critical claims at the source. 5. Record sample limits and deliver the reviewed table.
rubric: The brief names role, context and format
Only named public sources
Sample sizes and limits are recorded
Uncertain values carry a confidence label
A critical review precedes delivery
The format matches the CFO's table
Two hours cover a first analysis only

challenges.role: Sales lead at a 45-person trade business
challenges.scenario: 230 open quotations, some 90 days old, and nobody knows which are still live. Checking all by hand takes about three days. Build a review queue in two hours.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Export only customer reference, value, last activity and status, through the approved data process. 2. Define classes such as HOT, WARM, COLD and DEAD with fixed age and value thresholds. 3. Have follow-up drafts written for a person to approve; nothing goes out automatically. 4. Call the top records and queue the rest; never archive on a model rating alone. 5. Compare the rules with outcomes weekly.
rubric: Data comes from an export
Classes use named, reviewable thresholds
Each class has a plain-language draft
A person reviews high-value follow-ups
Two hours cover setup and drafts
A recurring weekly review
Customer data uses an approved access path

challenges.scenario: The monthly report has eight metrics, four departments and twelve commentary lines and takes six hours. Today a colleague is out and you have 90 minutes.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Set up a controlled workspace with the last three reports as structure and style reference. 2. Add current raw figures as a validated table. 3. Ask for the same structure, stated variance calculations and commentary that separates fact from hypothesis. 4. Recalculate every figure in Excel against its source cell. 5. Investigate two or three material variances and note possible explanations instead of one unevidenced cause. 6. Export in the required format.
rubric: Previous reports set structure and style
Every figure is checked apart from the prose
Variance rules are fixed before drafting
Explanations are marked as hypotheses
Checking gets more time than wording
The format matches management reporting
Workspace and checks are reusable next month

challenges.role: Executive assistant at a 200-person software company
challenges.scenario: An executive flies to an investor meeting tomorrow. By tonight you need an eight-page briefing on three competitors: finances, positioning, management, recent news and an evidence-based risk view.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Fix the pages first: one summary, two per competitor, one comparison. 2. Collect the same source categories per competitor, with date and link. 3. Draft against the template and mark every uncertain statement. 4. Check financial figures and quotes in the originals. 5. Compare financial strength, delivery pace, team and product, backing every rating. 6. Deliver the briefing and a one-page meeting reference.
rubric: The structure is fixed before drafting
Every competitor gets the same source plan
The writing follows an approved internal example
Figures and quotes are checked at the source
The matrix separates evidence from judgement
Briefing plus a one-page meeting reference
Four hours include time for checking

challenges.role: IT lead at a 60-person family business
challenges.scenario: Management asks where AI would pay off and wants a first concept next week. Time is short and the company has no AI practice yet.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: list candidate use cases and strike any without a process owner or data path. 2. Day 2: ask eight people from different functions five short questions about recurring work and failure points; let the model cluster the answers and check each cluster against the originals. 3. Day 3: compare the rest on effort, staff affected, data sensitivity, risk and time to evidence. 4. Propose two candidates with assumptions, controls and a next validation step; state benefits as ranges built from named inputs.
rubric: Research is combined with staff evidence
The model clusters and people decide
Effort, reach, risk and time are criteria
Only two prioritised candidates
The output fits on one decision page
Each candidate has an owner and a test
Three days leave time to check sources

challenges.role: Marketing lead at a 30-person B2B software company
challenges.scenario: You plan the Q3 LinkedIn calendar: three posts a week for 13 weeks on AI-native teams, with no agency budget and nobody else on it.
challenges.timeBudget: 1 day for the Q3 plan plus 30 minutes per week for drafting
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Analyse the last 30 posts and derive three repeatable formats; small samples prove no causation. 2. Have topics proposed for a German B2B audience and pick 39 without duplicates. 3. Fix each topic's angle and required evidence before any hook. 4. The calendar names owner, source status and review date. 5. Write three drafts a week and edit them for accuracy and company voice. 6. Review performance monthly and note what you change.
rubric: Past posts guide style without copying
Performance data is used with stated limits
Exactly 39 topics across 13 weeks
Angle and evidence come before drafting
The weekly 30 minutes cover drafting only
A monthly review records changes
Precise language for German B2B readers

challenges.scenario: Customers have asked for three competing features, and the next sprint has room for one. How do you decide and document the decision?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Record each request with customer context and usage data. 2. Note each feature's user problem, affected segments and existing workarounds. 3. Build a RICE table with written definitions; the model calculates only once inputs are checked. 4. Plan a small research step for each thinly evidenced estimate. 5. Record the decision, assumptions and rejected options. 6. After release, compare actual use with the estimates.
rubric: A documented method
Product-usage evidence is included
Confidence is stated and tied to evidence
Weak assumptions get a research step
Decision and rejected options are recorded
A post-release measurement point is set
The model calculates and the owner decides

challenges.role: Compliance officer at a medium-sized financial company
challenges.scenario: Management wants an AI chat assistant in customer advice. Within two weeks you justify whether and under which conditions it can proceed; GDPR, the EU AI Act and sector rules can all apply.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Describe system, user journey, decision effects, data categories, provider and human role. 2. Check each framework separately against primary sources: GDPR legal basis, minimisation and DPIA; EU AI Act role and risk class; financial-supervision rules. 3. List requirements, evidence and open questions. 4. Qualified legal and compliance owners review the analysis. 5. Build a decision matrix of permitted scope, prohibited uses, contracts, controls, tests and training. 6. Record the recommendation and its conditions; model output is not legal advice.
rubric: Each legal framework is checked separately
Primary sources support the summary
A qualified legal review is mandatory
The matrix separates scope, exclusions and conditions
Required evidence is named
Management gets a conditional recommendation
Risk-class decisions are documented for audit

challenges.role: HR lead at a 500-person industrial company
challenges.scenario: 370 applications in ten days for five vacancies. The team manages 20 a day and needs a lawful triage process by Friday, without handing employment decisions to a model.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Hiring owners set measurable requirements, evidence rules and prohibited proxy criteria per role before any model runs. 2. Confirm legal basis, retention, access, provider contract, EU AI Act classification and impact assessments. 3. Use AI only for approved admin work, such as pulling evidence into a review table; nothing is ranked or rejected automatically. 4. Recruiters read the source application and decide every case. 5. Test for extraction errors and disparate outcomes, edge cases included. 6. Keep an audit trail and the applicant-rights process.
rubric: Criteria and prohibited proxies are fixed first
Legal basis and AI Act class are checked
The model never ranks or rejects
A recruiter decides every case
Accuracy and bias tests cover edge cases
Retention and applicant rights are recorded
A review table with sources

challenges.role: Sales engineer at an enterprise B2B software company
challenges.scenario: An enterprise customer wants a technical proof of concept with access to its database in ten days; such work usually takes six weeks. Do you accept, and with what scope and controls?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: find comparable internal proofs of concept and record reusable parts with licence, owner and test state. 2. Days 1 and 2: agree five observable user stories, a data-access boundary, acceptance criteria and exclusions. 3. Days 3 to 7: build and test in an isolated environment and review generated code and dependencies. 4. Day 8: security and operations review of authentication, audit logs, rate limits, secrets and teardown. 5. Day 9: rehearse the demo and the failure path. 6. Day 10: show the agreed scope and record what production would need.
rubric: Reuse is checked first
Scope is capped at five user stories
A person reviews code and tests
Security controls and teardown are checked
An internal dry run precedes the customer
It is clearly separate from a production commitment
The plan names owners, gates and exclusions

challenges.role: Office manager at a 40-person law firm
challenges.scenario: The firm gets 120 client emails a day: 40 percent existing matters, 30 percent appointments, 20 percent new enquiries, 10 percent spam. Two people cannot keep up. Cut the work without exposing privileged information or sending unreviewed legal communication.
challenges.timeBudget: 1 week for setup plus continuous improvement
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Before choosing a model, settle what confidentiality, professional secrecy, retention and access require; local execution alone proves no compliance. 2. Build an isolated n8n workflow that sorts approved messages into four queues. 3. Appointment and acknowledgement replies stay drafts until authorised staff release them. 4. Existing matters and unclear messages go to the responsible team without generated legal advice. 5. Keep spam handling reversible during evaluation. 6. Review classification errors weekly against a fixed test set. 7. Document the assessment, processor roles, staff procedure and client information duties with qualified counsel.
rubric: The architecture follows professional secrecy
Classification routes and decides nothing legal
Authorised staff release every template
Unclear messages have a fixed path
A weekly error review uses a fixed test set
Legal and data-protection controls are documented
Counsel assesses client transparency duties

challenges.scenario: The 2027 plan fills 200 spreadsheet rows on targets, budget and team growth and used to take two weeks. You want two days without lowering the review standard.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1, morning: compare the last three plans with actuals and find categories with repeated forecast error. 2. Day 1, afternoon: record 2027 assumptions with source, owner and confidence, then build base, downside and upside scenarios. 3. Day 2, morning: functional leads challenge the assumptions and open risks are written down; the model can structure this but cannot validate a business assumption. 4. Day 2, afternoon: finish the workbook and a one-page summary per scenario. 5. Schedule quarterly plan-to-actual checks.
rubric: Past plan-to-actual gaps feed calibration
Three scenarios use stated assumptions
Functional leads challenge the assumptions
Each scenario has a one-page summary
Quarterly reviews compare actuals with the plan
The managing director stays accountable
Two days keep review and sign-off gates
